I've asked this question as well, but I sought out the answers through various sources. From what I understand, the Greeks didn't actually believe in the Gods of Olympus; they were just a nice story, and not unlike the Saints of Catholicism. For example, Athena was the goddess of wisdom and courage, while Hephaestus was the god of smithy and weaponry. So you might say a prayer to Athena and one the Hephaestus, but these were more symbolic worship to the overarching ideals that they represent; the "spirits" of battle, in other words. I don't know if that explains it too well though.

Essentially my takeaway was that the Greeks didn't think these gods/esses existed as actual physical manifestations; there was no Athena to hear their prayer. But rather they understood that these were aspects of the civilization they had built, and the spirit of these aspects was not to be taken for granted. War is nothing without weaponry; weaponry is useless without the knowledge of its use. Both are useless if your army/civilization isn't fed (Artemis for the harvest), the harvest won't happen without the sun (Apollo), etc.

So the gods and goddesses were more succinct, personified (more relatable) representations of these larger ideals of humanity, and from what I learned most Greeks thought of them like this, rather than actually believing in divine beings. Prayers were more out of respect, understanding, and reverence for these aspects of humanity and their importance.

It makes sense in my head anyway; I don't know if I've conveyed it very well though. Also that's just the Greeks. I think a lot of Christians today do believe that God is "just behind that cloud," peaking out at you when you're not looking.
